statement: Nemet’s worldwide PV price reconstruction, interpreted alongside US market examples, documents a 1970s shift from space to terrestrial applications with changing quality requirements, standardization and market structure; falling module prices alone do not measure factory learning.

sources.supports: Worldwide price series from two world surveys, used as a cost proxy; partly US market evidence about quality, customers and standardization; no causal allocation of the early residual.

counterevidence: Manufacturing improvements also occurred; terrestrial government purchases remained substantial.
inference_limits: No causal allocation of the 1975–1979 residual to quality, markups or standardization; niche procurement is not evidence of grid competitiveness.

test.mechanism_chain: New terrestrial tasks and customers -> less customized products and altered markups -> observed prices change with production practice.
test.strongest_rival: Repeated output alone lowers an unchanged product’s factory cost.
test.discriminating_observation: Do prices fall faster than the engineering model explains while customers/product requirements change?
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S01 §§3.1–3.2: early residual and market changes found; later period better explained.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Quality, competition and manufacturing changed together; no matched unchanged-product counterfactual.

statement: PV cost decomposition is model-sensitive: for 1980–2001 Nemet assigns 43% of decline to plant size, whereas Kavlak et al. assign 8%; the latter assigns 36% for 2001–2012 and separates efficiency, material use, prices and yield. Their reconstructions also identify early silicon supply/process benefits inherited from the semiconductor industry rather than generated entirely by PV output.

sources.supports: 43% plant-size allocation and semiconductor silicon-supply spillover.
8% and 36% plant-size allocations; revised cost equation; semiconductor supply/know-how before the mid-2000s transition.

counterevidence: Both studies support several improvement channels, but their shared historical evidence is not two independent estimates of the same causal policy effect.
inference_limits: These are allocated contributions under engineering models; neither percentage is a universal learning coefficient, electricity-price effect or welfare estimate. The comparison changes reconstructed inputs as well as model definitions (including the 1980 plant-size input); it does not isolate the cost equation as the cause of different shares.

test.reason: Reports and compares published model allocations, without treating them as identified causal effects.

statement: China’s emergence as a PV producer in the late 2000s did not imply similarly large domestic deployment: the inspected 2010 study reports over one-third of world production in 2008 with over 95% exported, and about 2.2% of global demand in 2009.

sources.supports: Production/export estimates and separate 2009 domestic-demand share.

counterevidence: The production and demand numbers concern different years and inherited industry estimates; domestic installations were not zero.
inference_limits: No current market claim and no subtraction of nonmatching denominators; production capacity, annual output and deployment must remain distinct.

test.reason: Dated production/export and demand observations establish a stage/geographic mismatch, not its causal magnitude.

statement: Interviews and supply-chain evidence from early Chinese PV entry support imported production equipment plus skilled personnel as important channels; upstream process secrecy and sparse equipment markets constrained entry despite downstream success.

sources.supports: Turnkey lines, vendor training, diaspora recruitment and segment-specific entry barriers.

counterevidence: Low wages, energy prices, finance and foreign deployment incentives also mattered; firms’ retrospective accounts may exaggerate chosen channels.
inference_limits: Small producer-centered sample, rough equipment competition measure and imperfect patent proxies; no estimate of independent policy or labour contribution.

test.mechanism_chain: Equipment purchases plus recruited expertise -> process operation/adaptation -> cell/module entry; upstream tacit processes remain harder to acquire.
test.strongest_rival: Cheap factors alone explain entry uniformly across supply-chain stages.
test.discriminating_observation: Downstream/upstream entry should differ with accessible equipment and tacit knowledge even within the same country.
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S03 contrasts stages, documents vendor training and returning executives, and reports later FDI following pioneer firms.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Stages also differ in capital intensity, energy use and market concentration; no controlled isolation.

statement: The 2016 seven-country reactor-cost compilation records differing within-country overnight-cost trajectories, including declines across Korean construction cohorts and escalation in later US/French cohorts; it does not identify a universal sign of nuclear learning.

sources.supports: Country/cohort construction-start comparisons and local-currency cost normalization.

counterevidence: Countries adopted different designs in different eras; data quality and coverage vary, and some prototype routes are excluded.
inference_limits: The 349-reactor sample is not all proposed projects. Korean cohort-count inconsistency is not resolved here; no precise Korean cohort total is asserted. No international cost ranking is inferred.

test.reason: Describes variation in the published construction-cost sample, without attributing it solely to standardization or state structure.

statement: France’s coordinated PWR programme combined bulk ordering, licensed designs, regulatory continuity and EDF engineering capacity with rapid deployment, yet its later construction cohorts still experienced real cost escalation.

sources.supports: Institutional organization, deployment timing, design changes and estimated escalation.
Later reactor-level series also shows escalation, with different magnitudes/coverage.

counterevidence: French cost magnitudes differ by reconstruction and cohort; national coordination did not mean unchanged designs or citizen consent.
inference_limits: The coordinated setting supports an enabling account, not proof of necessity or sufficiency. Grubler’s universal negative-learning generalization is rejected here.

test.mechanism_chain: Concentrated ordering and engineering authority -> repeatable build programme -> rapid capacity deployment.
test.strongest_rival: Falling unit costs are the necessary cause of rapid deployment.
test.discriminating_observation: Can deployment expand under coordinated procurement while real construction costs rise?
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S05 documents both rapid programme expansion and escalation; ENE-S04 supplies later, differently constructed French cost series.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Oil security, political priorities, financing and grid demand coincide; comparison does not identify each institutional contribution.

statement: In Eash-Gates et al.’s US four-loop-plant reconstruction for 1976–1987, indirect accounts contribute 72% of the modeled cost increase, placing engineering, supervision and construction organization alongside hardware and regulatory requirements.

sources.supports: 61 EEDB accounts; 72% indirect contribution; model/data limits.

counterevidence: Indirect accounts can themselves include responses to regulation, changed scope or schedules; the allocation does not establish a separate regulation-free cause.
inference_limits: Account attribution is not a causal estimate that management alone explains 72%; it covers one modeled configuration and interval, not every reactor or worker productivity level.

test.mechanism_chain: Complex site activities and changing execution conditions -> more engineering/support and installation burden -> higher constructed cost.
test.strongest_rival: Cost escalation is entirely additional reactor hardware demanded by safety rules.
test.discriminating_observation: Do indirect service accounts account for large changes beyond direct hardware expenditure?
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S06 EEDB decomposition found the majority in indirect accounts and acknowledges proportional-allocation assumptions.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Regulation, redesign and site interference can generate indirect costs jointly; ultimate causal shares remain underdetermined.

statement: Overnight reactor construction cost excludes interest during construction, and completed-project cost trajectories omit the outcome of cancellation; they cannot by themselves establish investor affordability or system welfare.

sources.supports: Explicit exclusion of IDC; distinction from electricity cost and coverage frame.
Reports 2017 abandonment of VC Summer as a separate project outcome.

counterevidence: Overnight costs remain useful for an explicitly restricted question about construction resource cost.
inference_limits: No claim that every omitted cost reverses any national ranking; social damages and avoided pollution are not estimated.

test.reason: States accounting and sampling boundaries, including an observed cancellation, without estimating their aggregate causal effect.

statement: Hoerni’s 1959 patent application specifies retaining a nonconducting surface coating over exposed junction edges; the museum history dates a working planar transistor to March 1959 and commercial introduction to April 1960.

sources.supports: Protected-junction process architecture.
Demonstration and commercialization chronology; subsequent reliability problems.

counterevidence: The process still needed complementary masking, diffusion, contacts and packaging; later bonding/interconnect failures continued.
inference_limits: Patent and retrospective chronology do not measure yield or prove that planar technology alone caused the semiconductor industry’s expansion.

test.mechanism_chain: Surface coating retained during fabrication -> junction protection -> reproducible planar-device architecture.
test.strongest_rival: A patent idea alone demonstrates commercially satisfactory production.
test.discriminating_observation: Is there separate evidence of functioning hardware and a later marketed device, as well as unresolved failure modes?
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S07 describes process; ENE-S14 records demonstration, commercial device and subsequent reliability issues.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Factory qualification and independent yield series were not inspected; museum history inherits the patent record.

statement: The Apollo computer programme supported an early IC production niche through a large, standardized NOR-gate purchase, while its engineers valued size, power, timing and reliability rather than the lowest initial component price.

sources.supports: Single-gate choice, initially higher cost, large 1963 production share and participant disagreement over perceived risk.

counterevidence: Other military and commercial customers existed; NASA history alone cannot establish its share of total industry cost decline.
inference_limits: Procurement volume supports demand creation in a specific niche, not a claim that NASA invented ICs or alone financed semiconductor diffusion; historical 60% estimate is not extrapolated.

test.mechanism_chain: Mission constraints plus financed programme -> standardized purchase and qualification effort -> early IC production at volume.
test.strongest_rival: Unsubsidized component cheapness already made the choice automatic.
test.discriminating_observation: Did designers choose higher-priced components for nonprice capabilities and create a large early order?
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S08 records higher initial IC cost, single NOR type and intensive 1963 purchasing.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Reliability choices and procurement size are jointly determined; no no-Apollo industry counterfactual.

statement: Irwin and Klenow’s 1974–1992 merchant-DRAM model estimates stronger own-firm than external learning contributions and finds no systematic faster learning rate for Japanese firms; it does not support a simple national-learning-superiority explanation.

sources.supports: 32-firm shipment/price dataset; own/external and Japanese-rate tests; ambiguous Japanese within-country spillover difference.

counterevidence: Tests of stronger within-Japan spillovers are inconclusive; international cooperation, investment and equipment differences may matter through other channels.
inference_limits: Costs and yields are not observed directly; structural competition assumptions and sample selection qualify the interpretation. Results concern merchant DRAM, not all chips or all eras.

test.mechanism_chain: Repeated firm production and some external knowledge -> lower inferred marginal cost -> product-generation price/output patterns.
test.strongest_rival: Japanese firms inherently learn faster, or domestic-only spillovers dominate.
test.discriminating_observation: Allow country-specific learning slopes and separate same-country from cross-country cumulative production.
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S09 estimates these alternatives, reporting similar country slopes and own-firm contribution about three times external contribution in baseline.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Unobserved investment, R&D and selection can covary with shipments; some spillover parameters are imprecise.

statement: The same DRAM study finds economically important spillovers between adjacent product generations in only two of seven tested transitions, so experience in one generation cannot be treated as a guaranteed permanent entry barrier.

sources.supports: Weak cross-generation effects and entry/exit examples.

counterevidence: Some spillovers are statistically detectable but economically tiny; capital, design skills, equipment and customer relationships can still deter entry.
inference_limits: Weak estimated spillovers are not evidence that experience or incumbency has no value; the underlying proprietary data were not re-estimated.

test.mechanism_chain: Design-generation change -> partial obsolescence of specific production knowledge -> limited transferable learning advantage.
test.strongest_rival: An early lead guarantees cumulatively increasing advantage across every generation.
test.discriminating_observation: Does previous-generation production strongly predict subsequent-generation cost, and do entrants appear despite little prior production?
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S09 Table 7 identifies only two economically meaningful transitions and discusses contemporaneous entry.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Model imposes a particular knowledge-depreciation structure; entry is selected and requires other assets.

statement: Yoshino’s account separates a rechargeable laboratory configuration from saleable batteries: polyacetylene’s heat/volume limitations motivated a carbon anode, and comparative impact testing supported continued development before Japanese commercialization in 1991.

sources.supports: PA limitations, carbon/lithiated-cathode combination, 1985 patent, impact comparison and 1991 commercialization.

counterevidence: This is a retrospective inventor narrative, not the whole industry’s development record or statistical safety certification.
inference_limits: A passed impact test does not establish general safety; commercial process yields, warranties, financing terms and all intervening qualification work remain unknown.

test.mechanism_chain: Portable-device demand and metallic-lithium/PA limitations -> paired material changes and safety tests -> candidate suitable for commercialization.
test.strongest_rival: Electrochemical charge/discharge demonstration alone suffices for market entry.
test.discriminating_observation: Are working configurations rejected on heat, size or abuse performance, followed by separate commercialization steps?
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S10 gives those rejected configurations and contrast tests, followed by commercialization date.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Narrative selection and retrospective credit cannot establish independent necessity of every contribution.

statement: For representative high-energy-density 18650 cells, Ziegler et al. compare 1995–2000 with 2010–2015 and allocate 38% of modeled cost decline to charge-density improvements; reduced material prices and nonmaterial costs also contribute.

sources.supports: Fixed-size cell definition, reconstructed costs and density/material decomposition.

counterevidence: Historical data are sparse and unequal across variables; some parameter values represent selected high-energy cells or prototypes, not a census.
inference_limits: USD per energy capacity differs from price per cell, pack cost, cycle life and power capability. The result does not cover LFP vehicle packs or all battery uses.

test.mechanism_chain: More active capacity in a fixed cell volume plus lower input cost -> overhead and components spread over more stored energy -> lower modeled USD/Wh.
test.strongest_rival: Raw-material cheapness or factory replication alone explains the decline.
test.discriminating_observation: Does a fixed-configuration component model require large energy-density changes as well as input-price changes?
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S11 separates those variables and finds a substantial charge-density contribution.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Component interactions and representative-cell selection mean decomposition is not intervention identification.

statement: The battery model’s baseline assigns about 54% of cost decline to broadly defined R&D, 30% to scale and 2% to learning-by-doing; these shares depend on classifications that include pilot-line and process work within R&D.

sources.supports: Definitions, baseline shares, alternative-assignment sensitivity and proprietary information limits.

counterevidence: The authors’ alternative assignments retain the broad ranking, but routine and nonroutine improvements can be complementary rather than mutually separable activities.
inference_limits: No inference that factory workers contributed only 2%, or that a public R&D programme caused 54%. Public/private R&D and endogenous demand are not independently identified.

test.mechanism_chain: Recorded component/process changes -> literature-based assignment to research, routine learning or scale -> estimated mechanism shares.
test.strongest_rival: A different classification of intertwined process work changes apparent research versus learning contributions.
test.discriminating_observation: Does the ranking survive plausible reassignments, and are records available to separate overlapping activities?
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S11 tests several extreme assignments and reports robust ranking but sparse/proprietary process evidence.
test.remaining_ambiguity: The method cannot identify a counterfactual public/private funding effect or labour’s social contribution.

statement: In China’s mid-2000s electric-two-wheeler market, lead-acid remained the dominant battery despite commercially available lithium-ion alternatives; a contemporary comparison estimated roughly fourfold upfront Li-ion battery cost with a longer assumed life.

sources.supports: VRLA dominance and limited advanced-battery availability; export mix uncertainty.
Approximate power-equivalent fourfold purchase price and two-to-threefold lifespan comparison.

counterevidence: Advanced-battery sales were increasing; estimated production shares include exports and are not domestic-use shares.
inference_limits: Does not prove low income or credit constraints caused individual choices. Historical price comparison is not a current specification, a universal lifetime ratio or a fully normalized lifecycle estimate.

test.reason: Establishes coexistence/continued older practice and reported price trade-off, leaving buyer-level causal attribution open.

statement: E-bike adoption in the surveyed Chinese cities combined component-based assembly with a policy-shaped choice set: motorcycle restrictions favored some electric use, while other cities restricted e-bikes; available surveys mainly observed substitution from bicycles and public transport.

sources.supports: Field methods, standardized components, six factory visits, motorcycle/e-bike bans, previous-mode observations.

counterevidence: Urban distance, incomes, transit quality and enforcement differed with policy; modular architecture did not eliminate entry/quality barriers.
inference_limits: Ten-city observations and three-city prior-mode surveys are not a national causal estimate. No inference that all Chinese adoption was voluntary or that bans alone explain it.

test.mechanism_chain: Standard components and permissive local classification amid motorcycle constraints -> accessible vehicle supply and usable road space -> adoption by some urban travellers.
test.strongest_rival: Uniform technical superiority or a uniform national mandate explains uptake.
test.discriminating_observation: Are rival modes and local restrictions heterogeneous, and are assemblers observed using standardized prefabricated parts?
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S12 documents opposing city rules, survey choice sets and six assembly-plant observations.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Policy adoption is endogenous to congestion and demand; force-field rankings do not identify effects.

statement: The 2009 partial lifecycle analysis finds that e-bike comparisons depend on regional electricity and the displaced mode; lead emissions arise upstream in battery production/recycling, so zero tailpipe emissions do not demonstrate zero pollution or a quantified health benefit.

sources.supports: Production/grid inventories, lead pathways, excluded lifecycle processes, absence of direct population health measures.

counterevidence: E-bikes compare favorably with some motorized alternatives on several modeled emissions metrics; emissions relocation can reduce urban exposure while imposing burdens elsewhere.
inference_limits: Mass emissions are not absorbed dose, disease or money damages. Old lead-flow factors, borrowed vehicle factors, load/lifespan assumptions and omitted processes prevent a full welfare estimate.

test.mechanism_chain: Battery manufacture/recycling and electricity use -> geographically redistributed pollution -> different lifecycle comparisons than tailpipe accounting.
test.strongest_rival: A vehicle without exhaust has negligible pollution regardless of energy/material supply chain or displaced travel.
test.discriminating_observation: Include lead flows and region-specific electricity; compare bicycle, bus, motorcycle and car rather than one favorable alternative.
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S13 performs a partial inventory and explicitly states missing health and lifecycle evidence.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Magnitude and exposure depend on process controls, region, service life and counterfactual travel; some inputs predate rapid e-bike expansion.
